recent_posts.title: Guard rails, not gatekeeping
recent_posts.summary: Agentic coding tools are enabling more people to contribute to software projects, but some experienced developers respond with gatekeeping. A better approach is setting up automated guard rails: formatters (Standard for Ruby, Ruff for Python), security scanners (Brakeman, Bandit, Gitleaks), and pre-commit hooks running before code is pushed. These checks catch mechanical issues automatically, freeing human reviewers to focus on design, intent, and architecture. The same tools benefit all contributors — humans and AI agents alike — and make it easier to maintain quality without excluding newcomers.

recent_posts.title: Superpowers have changed how I write software (mostly)
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares how the Superpowers skill set for Claude Code has transformed their agentic coding workflow. The workflow centers on three stages: brainstorming with the agent to clarify requirements and build shared context, generating a human-readable Markdown plan, and executing that plan. The author argues that the real value isn't automation but the structured brainstorming that forces critical thinking before any code is written—mirroring good software development habits. Practical notes include hitting token limits on Claude Code Pro and upgrading to Max, plus a real-world example of using the workflow to organize Obsidian notes.

recent_posts.title: Everyday Rails is now Left of the Dev
recent_posts.summary: A developer announces the rebranding of their blog from Everyday Rails to Left of the Dev, reflecting their career evolution from exclusive Rails work (2007-2022) to managing diverse legacy systems in Python, Go, and Ruby at O'Reilly. The author now focuses on modernizing old codebases without complete rewrites while pursuing game development in Lua through Bandageman Studios. The rebrand enables broader content beyond Rails, addressing topics like legacy system maintenance, multi-language development, and independent software creation.

recent_posts.title: Newly open-sourced development setup tools
recent_posts.summary: Aaron Sumner shares his open-sourced development setup tools following a laptop disaster, emphasizing the use of chezmoi for managing dotfiles, the ruralocity/gh-clone-team-repos tool for cloning team repositories, and the mise-en-place tool for managing Rubies, Nodes, and environment configurations. The goal is to simplify workstation setups and improve workflow efficiency.

recent_posts.title: Notes on pair programming with Aider when Python isn't readily available
recent_posts.summary: Aider is an open source, terminal-based AI pair programming tool that provides an alternative to GitHub Copilot Chat. It integrates with your application's git repository to make context-aware coding suggestions and can handle file operations. Aider is a Python application that can be installed using the uv tool, making it convenient for environments without native Python support. It is compatible with various AI models and offers spending transparency by showing token and money costs for each response.

top_posts.title: A few things I've learned to simplify working in dev containers
top_posts.summary: VS Code's top-notch support for dev containers is the feature that keeps me using it these days, over other editors or IDEs. If VS Code isn't your cup of tea, you can try the standalone command line application or check out Microsoft’s opened Development Containers specification for a more editor-agnostic approach.
